title: DP: Word Break
oneLiner: Can a string be split into dictionary words? dp[i] says whether the first i characters can; it is true if some earlier split point j is true and s[j..i) is a word.
keyTakeaway: Let dp[i] mean "the prefix of length i can be segmented". dp[0] is true (the empty prefix). dp[i] is true if for some j < i, dp[j] is true and s[j..i) is in the dictionary (a hash set). The answer is dp[n]. O(n²) substring checks (times the substring length), O(n) table.
explanation:
Given a string s and a list of words, return true if s can be split into a sequence of one or more dictionary words, using a word as many times as you like. "applepenapple" with ["apple", "pen"] is true (apple pen apple). "catsandog" with ["cats", "dog", "sand", "and", "cat"] is false: cats and leaves og, cat sand leaves og.

Plain recursion tries every first word and recurses on the rest. It is correct but exponential, because the same suffix gets re-solved down many paths: in "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaab" with ["a", "aa", "aaa"] it explores a huge number of splits before discovering the b makes all of them fail. The rest of the string only depends on where you are, not how you got there, which is the signal for DP.

Define dp[i] = whether s[0..i), the first i characters, can be segmented. dp[0] = true: the empty prefix needs no words. For each i from 1 to n, look at every split point j < i: if dp[j] is true and the piece s[j..i) is a dictionary word, then dp[i] is true and you can stop looking. Put the words in a hash set first so each lookup is O(1) on average (plus hashing the substring).

There are O(n²) pairs (j, i), and building each substring costs up to its length, so O(n³) in the worst case, often described as O(n²) lookups. You can cut this by only trying lengths up to the longest word. The table is O(n). Note that the empty string is trivially true here: zero words.

The visualization fills dp for "leetcode" with ["leet", "code"]. The array shows dp[0..8] as 1 (true) and 0 (false).

starterCode.python:
def word_break(s, word_dict):
    words = set(word_dict)
    dp = [False] * (len(s) + 1)  # dp[i]: the first i characters can be segmented
    dp[0] = True
    # TODO: for i from 1 to len(s), for j from 0 to i - 1:
    # if dp[j] and s[j:i] in words, set dp[i] = True and stop trying j.
    return False

visualizationSteps.message: s = "leetcode", words = ["leet", "code"]. dp[0] = 1: the empty prefix needs no words.
dp[2]: no split point j has dp[j] true and s[j..2) in the dictionary, so "le" can't be split. dp[2] stays 0.
dp[4]: dp[0] is true and "leet" is a word, so the first 4 characters "leet" can be split. dp[4] = 1.
dp[6]: no split point j has dp[j] true and s[j..6) in the dictionary, so "leetco" can't be split. dp[6] stays 0.
dp[8]: dp[4] is true and "code" is a word, so the first 8 characters "leetcode" can be split. dp[8] = 1.

recognitionSignals: "Can the string be split, segmented or built from these pieces?"
Recursion on "the rest of the string" where the same suffix is reached many ways.
A yes or no question over prefixes: dp over the prefix length.
gotchas: dp has n + 1 entries; dp[i] is about the first i characters, so the piece is s[j..i) (C# s[j..i], Python s[j:i]).
Forgetting dp[0] = true means nothing can ever become true.
Checking only the longest or the first matching word greedily fails ("cars" with ["car", "ca", "rs"] needs ca + rs).
confusableWith: Coin Change asks for the fewest pieces summing to an amount; Word Break asks only whether the pieces can cover the string, and pieces must match the text exactly.
Decode Ways also walks prefixes, but counts the splits and each piece is one or two digits.

complexity.note: There are about n²/2 (j, i) pairs, each a hash-set lookup. Strictly, building and hashing each substring costs up to its length, so the worst case is O(n³); limiting j to the longest word length tightens it. The dp table is n + 1 booleans, plus the word set.
